recommendations.ddl: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_events_user_id_created_at ON public.events (user_id, created_at DESC);
recommendations.reason: Adds ~60 MB and a write-path cost on an insert-heavy table; acceptable given the index removes ~93M tuple reads per window from the top query. Build with CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking writes (it takes two table passes and can fail leaving an INVALID index — re-drop and retry if so). Note the DESC ordering is cosmetic here: a plain (user_id, created_at) btree can be scanned backwards at the same cost; keep DESC only for clarity. Follow-up (out of scope for this candidate): once this index is live, idx_events_created_at's 401 scans should largely migrate to it, but do NOT drop it yet — an ad-hoc 'SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE created_at > now()-interval $1' still range-scans created_at alone; re-evaluate after a full observation window.
evidence: pg_stat_statements: 'Activity feed' query (SELECT type, source, created_at FROM events WHERE user_id=$1 AND created_at > now()-interval $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $3) is the #1 statement by total time — 400 calls, 52.68 ms mean, 21,071 ms total.
Matching app catalog entry events_recent_by_user.sql confirms this is a live, high-frequency application query (~400 calls/window), not an ad-hoc one.

Current plan (EXPLAIN): Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan on events, Bitmap Index Scan on idx_events_created_at with Index Cond on created_at only and 'Filter: (user_id = $1)' applied after the read; estimated 172,098 index rows fetched per execution; total cost 31,002.43.

Index stats corroborate the read amplification: idx_events_created_at has idx_scan=401 and idx_tup_read=93,654,234 (~233k tuples per scan) while the query returns ~1 row/call (465 rows over 400 calls).

HypoPG test of CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id, created_at DESC): planner_used_it=true; plan becomes 'Index Scan using <hypo> ... Index Cond: ((user_id = $1) AND (created_at > now() - interval))' with cost 0.06..8.08 — a ~3,800x planner cost reduction vs 31,002.

Alternative tested: (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (type, source) yields an Index Only Scan at the identical cost (8.08), so the extra payload columns buy no planner benefit and only add write/size overhead — plain 2-column index chosen.
Selectivity check: events has 2,000,000 live rows (193 MB heap) and pg_stats n_distinct=185,818 for user_id → ~11 rows per user, so the leading user_id column is highly selective.
events.seq_scan=0, confirming the cost is hidden inside index reads rather than sequential scans (triage rationale independently verified).

recommendations.ddl: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id_created_at ON public.orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
recommendations.reason: Adds ~7-9 MB of index and a small write cost on orders INSERT/UPDATE; acceptable given the table is 20 MB and the query is on every profile visit. With only ~2 rows per user today the trailing created_at column is not strictly required (a plain (user_id) index plans identically), but it costs little and keeps the ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT satisfied without a sort as per-user order counts grow. Existing idx_orders_created_at must be kept — orders_recent.sql (ops dashboard, 300 calls) depends on it. Build with CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking writes; if the build fails it leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped and retried.
evidence: pg_indexes on orders shows only orders_pkey (id) and idx_orders_created_at (created_at) — no index leads with user_id, so WHERE user_id=$1 has no usable access path.
Current plan for 'SELECT id,status,total_cents,created_at FROM orders WHERE user_id=$1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20': Parallel Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..4705.88) + Sort, total cost 5706.02.

HypoPG: with hypothetical btree (user_id, created_at DESC) the planner switches to Bitmap Index Scan on the new index (Index Cond: user_id = $1), total cost 11.93 — ~478x cheaper than 5706.02; planner_used_it = true.

pg_stat_statements: this exact statement runs 1200 calls, mean 7.97 ms, 9567 ms total — 3rd largest total_time in the window; app catalog confirms it as orders_by_user.sql ('Order history page: every profile visit').
pg_stat_user_tables for orders: seq_scan=2201, seq_tup_read=361,200,000 on a 300,000-row / 20 MB table (~164k rows per scan), idx_scan only 300 (the ops-dashboard ORDER BY created_at query).
Selectivity check: 300,000 orders across 155,278 distinct user_id (avg 1.93, max 9 rows per user) — a per-user lookup returns a handful of rows, ideal for a btree on user_id.

Alternatives tested: plain (user_id) and covering (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status,total_cents) both produce the identical 11.93 plan; the INCLUDE variant buys no index-only scan here, so the two-column form is chosen as the smallest index that also guarantees ordered retrieval.

recommendations.rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_order_items_order_id ON public.order_items USING btree (order_id);
recommendations.reason: Low risk. The two indexes are provably identical in the catalog (same AM, key columns, opclass, collation, indoption, no INCLUDE/predicate/expression), so the retained idx_order_items_order can satisfy every plan the dropped one could, and EXPLAIN confirms the sole order_items query already uses the retained one. Neither backs a constraint. Direction matters: drop idx_order_items_order_id (0 scans) and keep idx_order_items_order (1500 scans) — dropping the used one would be equally safe functionally but would invalidate cached plans and lose warm cache for no reason. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on a hot 900k-row table; note it cannot run inside a transaction block and, if it fails, can leave an INVALID index that must be dropped again. Rollback is a plain CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Separately (out of scope for C5): order_items_pkey also shows idx_scan=0, but it enforces the primary key and must be kept.
evidence: pg_index catalog comparison shows the two indexes are byte-for-byte equivalent, not just similar text: both amname=btree, indnatts=1, indnkeyatts=1 (no INCLUDE columns), indisunique=false, is_partial=false, has_expr=false, opclasses='3124' (int8_ops), collations='0', indoption='0' (same ASC/NULLS LAST sort order).

inspect_index on idx_order_items_order_id: backing_constraint=null, constraint_type=null, is_unique=false, is_primary=false — it backs no PK/UNIQUE/FK-supporting constraint, so dropping it cannot break a constraint or a REPLICA IDENTITY.

pg_stat_user_indexes on order_items: idx_order_items_order idx_scan=1500 / idx_tup_read=4502, while idx_order_items_order_id idx_scan=0 / idx_tup_read=0 — the planner has consistently chosen the sibling, never this one.

EXPLAIN of the app query 'SELECT product_id, qty FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1' plans Bitmap Index Scan on idx_order_items_order (cost=0.00..4.46, total 20.21) — the retained index already serves the only order_items access path, so the plan is unchanged after the drop.

list_app_queries contains exactly one order_items query (order_items_by_order.sql, ~1500 calls/window, WHERE order_id = $1, no ORDER BY, no partial predicate). No rare/cron job in the catalog references order_items at all, so the zero scan count is not a short-window artifact.
Both indexes are 17 MB on a 900,000-row table; the drop reclaims 17 MB and removes one duplicate index insert/HOT-miss maintenance path per write.

recommendations.ddl: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_products_price;
recommendations.rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_products_price ON public.products USING btree (price_cents);
recommendations.reason: Residual risk is an ad-hoc/BI/admin price-range query (e.g. WHERE price_cents BETWEEN ..., ORDER BY price_cents) that runs outside the instrumented app catalog and outside the 44-hour window; such a query would fall back to a seq scan on 800k rows. This is acceptable because the index is non-unique, backs no constraint, and no foreign key references price_cents, so dropping it cannot break correctness — only plan shape. Rollback is a single non-blocking CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY (not plain DROP) to avoid taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on products; note it cannot run inside a transaction block. Adjacent observation, not part of this candidate: idx_products_category (5080 kB) also shows 0 scans and no catalog query filters on category — worth raising as its own candidate rather than bundling here.
evidence: inspect_index: idx_products_price = CREATE INDEX ON public.products USING btree (price_cents), 20 MB, idx_scan=0, is_unique=false, is_primary=false, backing_constraint=null, partial_predicate=null — so no constraint or uniqueness guarantee depends on it.

list_app_queries: only two queries touch products — product_by_sku.sql (WHERE sku = $1) and products_by_ids.sql (WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[])). price_cents appears only in SELECT output lists, never in a WHERE, ORDER BY, or range predicate. No rare/cron job in the catalog references price_cents (contrast with dunning_job.sql, which the catalog explicitly flags as depending on idx_invoices_unpaid_due).

pg_stat_user_tables(products): idx_scan=2000 total. Per-index breakdown: products_pkey=1200 scans, products_sku_key=800 scans, sum=2000 — the entire index traffic is accounted for by the PK and SKU indexes, leaving exactly zero attributable to idx_products_price.

pg_stat_statements: products queries are product_by_sku (800 calls, 0.25 ms mean) and products_by_ids (400 calls, 0.26 ms mean); call counts align with the 800/1200 scans on sku/pkey. No price-filtered or price-ordered statement appears anywhere in the top-20 by total time.
Observation window is 1 day 20 hours (pg_stat_database.stats_reset = 2026-08-28T16:54:31Z), not a short burst — zero scans over ~44 hours covering all 17 catalogued app queries.

Table is read-only in this window (n_tup_ins=0, n_tup_upd=0, n_tup_del=0), so the index costs 20 MB of storage/cache/backup footprint now and would add write amplification on any future catalog price updates.

recommendations.ddl: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_events_type;
recommendations.rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_events_type ON public.events USING btree (type);
recommendations.reason: Risk is low: the index is non-unique, non-partial and backs no constraint, so dropping it cannot break data integrity or a FK. The residual risk is an unlogged ad-hoc/analyst query filtering on type that never reaches pg_stat_statements or the catalog; because type has only 8 distinct values (~250k rows each), such a query would get a bitmap scan of marginal benefit over a seq scan, and the index can be rebuilt CONCURRENTLY in minutes if needed. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY so no long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is taken on a high-insert table. Benefit: 12 MB reclaimed plus one less index to maintain on every INSERT into a 2M-row append-heavy table. Note the counters were reset recently (n_tup_ins = 0 for events), so zero scans alone was not sufficient — the verdict rests on the app catalog and query-stats absence of any predicate on type. Sibling finding worth triaging separately: idx_events_source (12 MB, 0 scans, 5 distinct values) is unused for exactly the same reasons.
evidence: inspect_index: idx_events_type = CREATE INDEX idx_events_type ON public.events USING btree (type); 12 MB, idx_scan = 0, is_unique = false, is_primary = false, partial_predicate = null, backing_constraint = null — it enforces no constraint.

list_app_queries: the only events query in the entire catalog is events_recent_by_user.sql (SELECT type, source, created_at FROM events WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100). 'type' appears only in the SELECT list, never in a WHERE/ORDER BY/JOIN clause. No cron/monthly job touches events at all.
pg_stat_statements: the only recurring events statement is that same activity-feed query (400 calls, 21.1 s total); no statement in the window filters or sorts on events.type.
EXPLAIN of the activity-feed query uses idx_events_created_at (Bitmap Index Scan, cost 0..3870.84) with user_id applied as a heap Filter — idx_events_type plays no part in the plan.

pg_stats: events.type has n_distinct = 8 over 2,000,000 live rows (~250k rows per value); EXPLAIN of a synthetic 'WHERE type = ''purchase''' estimates 244,533 rows at cost 30425 — a low-selectivity access path of little value even if such a query were introduced.

pg_stat_user_indexes on events: idx_events_created_at has 401 scans while both idx_events_type and idx_events_source sit at 0 scans; events_pkey (43 MB) also 0 scans but is the PK constraint and must stay.

recommendations.ddl: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_products_category;
recommendations.rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_products_category ON public.products USING btree (category);
recommendations.reason: Drop confirmed, but the triage RATIONALE is wrong and should not be recorded as the justification. It claims low cardinality means 'the planner may never use it even if a query exists.' I tested that directly: EXPLAIN on 'SELECT id, name, price_cents FROM products WHERE category = $1' DOES choose Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_category (cost 1095.42..9917.42, est. 100000 rows) over a seq scan. pg_stats shows category n_distinct = 8 over 800k rows (~12.5% selectivity), which is still cheap enough for a bitmap scan. So the index is usable — it is simply unused, because no query in the app catalog or in pg_stat_statements filters on category. The drop is justified purely by 'no consumer exists', not by 'the planner would reject it'. Practical risk: if anyone later adds a category-browse or category-facet query (a plausible feature on a products table), that query will regress to a seq scan of 800k rows and the index must be rebuilt — the rollback DDL does this online. Benefit is modest: only 5 MB reclaimed plus a small write-amplification saving on product inserts/updates, hence severity info rather than warning. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY so no ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is taken on products. Out of scope but noted for triage: idx_products_price (20 MB) also shows 0 scans with no matching catalog query and is a larger win than this candidate.
evidence: inspect_index: idx_products_category = CREATE INDEX ... USING btree (category), 5080 kB, idx_scan = 0, is_unique = false, is_primary = false, partial_predicate = null, backing_constraint = null — it enforces no constraint, so dropping it cannot break data integrity.

list_app_queries (full catalog, 17 queries incl. the rare monthly dunning cron): NO query filters, sorts, or groups by products.category. The only two products queries are product_by_sku (WHERE sku = $1) and products_by_ids (WHERE id = ANY($1)). product_by_sku returns category in the SELECT list but does not predicate on it, so it cannot use this index.

get_query_stats: the only products statements in the window are 'WHERE sku = $1' (800 calls, 0.25 ms mean) and 'WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[])' (400 calls, 0.26 ms mean). No category predicate appears in pg_stat_statements at all.

pg_index/pg_stat_user_indexes on products: products_pkey (17 MB, 1200 scans) and products_sku_key (24 MB, 800 scans) fully serve both live query patterns. inspect_index also reports table_seq_scans = 0, so no fallback sequential scan is compensating for a missing category path — the workload genuinely never touches category.
Non-unique, non-partial, no FK can reference it (a foreign key target must be unique), and no constraint depends on it — no hidden catalog dependency blocks the drop.

recommendations.rollback: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_events_source ON public.events USING btree (source);
recommendations.reason: Risk is that an ad-hoc/analyst query outside both the app catalog and the stats window filters on events.source; such a query would fall back to a seq scan on a 2M-row table. This is acceptable because the index is non-constraint, non-unique, zero-scan, and rebuild is a single CONCURRENTLY statement (~12 MB, no exclusive lock). Note idx_events_created_at is the only useful index here today and must be retained; also, the activity-feed query is the slowest statement in the window (52.7 ms mean) and would be better served by a composite (user_id, created_at DESC) index — that is a separate finding and is unaffected by this drop. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking writes on events.
evidence: inspect_index: idx_events_source = CREATE INDEX idx_events_source ON public.events USING btree (source), 12 MB, idx_scan = 0, is_unique=false, is_primary=false, partial_predicate=null, backing_constraint=null — it backs no constraint and enforces no uniqueness, so dropping it cannot break data integrity.

list_app_queries (full catalog, 17 queries incl. rare cron jobs like dunning_job.sql): only one query touches the events table — events_recent_by_user.sql: 'SELECT type, source, created_at FROM events WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval ... ORDER BY created_at DESC'. 'source' appears only in the SELECT list; no query filters, joins, sorts or groups on events.source. No scheduled/rare job references it.
pg_stat_statements: the only events queries in the window are the activity feed (400 calls) and a one-off 'SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE created_at > ...'. Neither can use a btree on (source).

EXPLAIN of the activity-feed query chooses Bitmap Index Scan on idx_events_created_at (Index Cond: created_at > now()-'7 days'); idx_events_source appears nowhere in the plan — a single-column index on (source) cannot serve as a covering index for a predicate on user_id/created_at.

pg_stat_user_indexes on events: idx_events_created_at has 401 scans (59 MB) and is the live access path; events_pkey, idx_events_type and idx_events_source all show 0 scans. Dropping idx_events_source removes 12 MB and one index maintenance write per row inserted into the 2M-row events table.

recommendations.rollback: No rollback is required or possible — REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds identical index contents and swaps atomically; the PRIMARY KEY constraint and its definition are unchanged. If the rebuild fails midway it leaves an INVALID index: verify with SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid='messages'::regclass; and clean up with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY public.messages_pkey_ccnew; then re-run.
recommendations.reason: Bloat is real and confirmed by direct pgstattuple measurement, so the triage rationale holds — but I am downgrading severity to info because the business impact is small. The index is never used for reads (no query in the catalog or pg_stat_statements looks up messages by id, and no FK references it), so the only benefit is reclaiming ~15 MB of disk and marginally cheaper insert-time uniqueness checks. It is not a latency fix. Recovering 15 MB on a database whose messages heap alone is 72 MB does not justify urgency; batch this with other maintenance rather than scheduling an emergency window. Execution risks: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on a PK is safe on PG12+ and does not block reads or writes, but it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock briefly at the final swap, so run it off-peak and expect it to abort if it cannot acquire that lock behind a long-running transaction. It also needs transient disk headroom for a second copy of the index (~20 MB) and can leave an INVALID *_ccnew index if interrupted, which must be dropped manually. Note the non-obvious trap: idx_scan = 0 would normally argue for DROP over REINDEX, but this index backs the PRIMARY KEY constraint and dropping it is not an option.
evidence: pgstatindex('messages_pkey') reports avg_leaf_density = 18.25% — far below the healthy live-btree band of 65-75%, and well under the ~55% action threshold. This is direct measurement, not an estimator.

Physical shape confirms it: 2459 leaf_pages / 20,234,240 bytes for 180,000 bigint entries = ~73 entries per 8 KB page. A packed btree page holds ~360-400 bigint entries, so the index occupies roughly 5x the pages its live entries require (~490 leaf pages / ~4 MB expected).
leaf_fragmentation = 0, empty_pages = 0, deleted_pages = 0 — the wasted space is sparse in-page fill, exactly the condition REINDEX rebuilds away, not free pages awaiting reuse by VACUUM.

pg_stat_user_tables for messages: n_dead_tup = 0, n_tup_upd = 0, n_tup_del = 0, autovacuum_count = 0. The low density is not from ongoing row churn, so a one-time rebuild is durable and VACUUM is not the correct remedy.

Index cannot be dropped despite idx_scan = 0: inspect_index shows is_primary = true, is_unique = true, backing_constraint = messages_pkey, constraint_type = 'p'. It enforces the PRIMARY KEY (id) uniqueness check on every INSERT.

idx_scan = 0 is expected rather than damning here — pg_constraint shows no FK references messages.id, and both catalogued messages queries (messages_by_thread.sql ~800 calls, messages_by_sender.sql ~600 calls) filter on thread_id/sender_id, never id. No read path uses the PK, which is why the fix is low-impact.
pg_class.reloptions is NULL for messages_pkey, so a non-default fillfactor does NOT explain the 18.25% density.

recommendations.rollback: No rollback needed — REINDEX rebuilds the identical definition (CREATE INDEX idx_messages_sender ON public.messages USING btree (sender_id)). If REINDEX CONCURRENTLY fails mid-flight it leaves an invalid idx_messages_sender_ccnew; remove it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY public.idx_messages_sender_ccnew; the original index stays valid throughout.
recommendations.reason: The triage rationale reached the right conclusion via partly weak reasoning (the '87 bytes/row' heuristic is unreliable for deduplicated btrees), but the independent pgstatindex measurement confirms real bloat: 22.21% density with 49.49% fragmentation. Risk of acting is low — REINDEX CONCURRENTLY takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes to messages continue, and this is a 15 MB index on a 72 MB heap, so the rebuild is fast. It needs transient disk space for a second copy (~15 MB) and will wait for long-running transactions to drain, so avoid running it during long analytics transactions. If interrupted it can leave an invalid _ccnew index that wastes space and must be dropped, but the original remains valid so no query regresses. Doing nothing is not dangerous — results stay correct and the current plan is already cheap — the cost is ~11 MB wasted plus extra buffer-cache pressure and I/O across ~600 scans per window. Because there is zero update/delete churn on this table, the bloat should not recur, so this is a one-off fix rather than a recurring maintenance job.
evidence: pgstatindex('idx_messages_sender') reports avg_leaf_density = 22.21%, far below the 65-75% healthy fill range and well under the ~55% reindex threshold.
pgstatindex also reports leaf_fragmentation = 49.49%, so leaf pages are both sparsely filled and out of physical order — a rebuild fixes both.

Page math confirms the estimator rather than contradicting it: 1853 leaf_pages hold 180,000 entries. At normal ~90% fill a bigint btree of that entry count needs roughly 460-500 leaf pages, so the index occupies ~4x the pages its live entries require. Expected post-rebuild size ~4 MB vs 15,245,312 bytes today (~11 MB reclaimed).
Structure is otherwise clean — empty_pages = 0 and deleted_pages = 0 — so the wasted space is inside partially-filled leaf pages, which only a rebuild can compact.
The index is genuinely used, so drop is the wrong action: inspect_index shows idx_scan = 600 and table_seq_scans = 0 on messages.

The app catalog contains a matching hot query, messages_by_sender.sql (~600 calls/window): SELECT thread_id, body, created_at FROM messages WHERE sender_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 — the WHERE column matches the indexed column exactly and the call count matches idx_scan = 600.
EXPLAIN of that query confirms live dependence: 'Index Scan using idx_messages_sender on messages, Index Cond: (sender_id = $1)' (cost=0.42..12.45).

sender_id is highly selective — 118,627 distinct senders over 180,000 rows (~1.5 rows/value) — so this is a legitimately useful index worth keeping and rebuilding, not a low-cardinality index to discard.

VACUUM would not help: pg_stat_user_tables for messages shows n_dead_tup = 0, n_tup_upd = 0, n_tup_del = 0, autovacuum_count = 0 — there are no dead tuples to reclaim, so the bloat is build/load-history related, not churn.

recommendations.ddl:
VACUUM (ANALYZE, VERBOSE) audit_logs;
ALTER TABLE audit_logs SET (autovacuum_enabled = true);
recommendations.rollback: ALTER TABLE audit_logs RESET (autovacuum_enabled); -- or SET (autovacuum_enabled = false) to restore the exact prior setting. The VACUUM itself only reclaims dead space and refreshes statistics; it is not reversible and needs no rollback.
recommendations.reason: MODIFIED from the original hypothesis in two ways. (1) Root cause corrected: triage suspected autovacuum thresholds were blocking, but autovacuum_enabled=false is set directly on the table, so a one-off VACUUM alone would let it silently re-bloat to the same state — the storage parameter must be reverted or this finding recurs. (2) The 28 MB of indexes must NOT be reindexed: avg_leaf_density 83.12% is healthy fill and a REINDEX would be wasted I/O; the fix is heap-side only. Before flipping autovacuum_enabled back on, confirm with the owning team why it was disabled — the usual reason is a bulk-load or retention job avoiding vacuum contention. If that job still exists, prefer per-table tuning (higher autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay or scale_factor) over leaving autovacuum off entirely, since an append-only audit table left unvacuumed also accumulates transaction-ID freeze debt. Plain VACUUM takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, runs concurrently with reads and writes, and is safe online. Deliberately NOT recommending VACUUM FULL, which would take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for no benefit on a 50 MB heap whose free space will be reused by future inserts.
evidence: pgstattuple('audit_logs'): dead_tuple_count=237898, dead_tuple_percent=32.9, dead_tuple_len=17,128,656 bytes, free_percent only 6.23 — dead space is real and not yet reclaimable. This corrects the triage figure of 280,000/41.18%, which came from the n_dead_tup estimator.
pg_class.reloptions for audit_logs = {autovacuum_enabled=false} — autovacuum is explicitly DISABLED on this table. This, not threshold tuning, is why it never ran.

Global settings are healthy: autovacuum=on, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold=50, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.2. At 400k live rows the trigger is ~80,050 dead tuples, far below the 237,898 present — the table would have been vacuumed long ago if not overridden.
pg_stat_user_tables: last_vacuum=NULL, last_autovacuum=NULL, vacuum_count=0, autovacuum_count=0 (only a single manual ANALYZE on 2026-08-28) — confirms zero vacuum history.

pg_stat_user_indexes for idx_audit_logs_actor: idx_scan=300, idx_tup_read=1043, idx_tup_fetch=0 — index entries are read then discarded at the heap visibility check, the signature of index pointers to dead heap tuples.
Sequential access is inflated by the dead rows: seq_scan=2 with seq_tup_read=1,275,796 (~638k tuples per scan vs only 400,000 live rows).

REINDEX REJECTED: pgstatindex('idx_audit_logs_actor') shows avg_leaf_density=83.12%, empty_pages=0, deleted_pages=0, tree_level=2 — a dense healthy btree far above the ~55% bloat threshold, so the 28 MB of indexes need no rebuild.

app_query_catalog audit_by_actor.sql (SELECT action, detail, created_at FROM audit_logs WHERE actor_id=$1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100, ~300 calls/window) is the active consumer; EXPLAIN shows Bitmap Index Scan on idx_audit_logs_actor -> Bitmap Heap Scan with Recheck Cond, so it pays the dead-tuple heap-visit cost directly.
pg_class: heap 50 MB / relpages=6356, age(relfrozenxid)=77 — no transaction-ID wraparound urgency, so this can be scheduled normally rather than as an emergency.
pg_stats: page_views.site_id has n_distinct=2 with MCV frequencies {2:0.5004, 1:0.4996} — every predicate value matches ~50% of the 200,000 live rows, so no btree can be selective.

HypoPG test of 'CREATE INDEX ON page_views (site_id)' for 'SELECT count(*) FROM page_views WHERE site_id=$1': planner_used_it=false; plan identical before/after (Finalize Aggregate cost=4059.76 -> Parallel Seq Scan on page_views cost=0.00..2912.59 rows=58824).
HypoPG test of composite 'CREATE INDEX ON page_views (site_id, viewed_at)': planner_used_it=false, same Parallel Seq Scan cost=4059.76 — no index-only-scan path was cheaper.
HypoPG test of partial 'CREATE INDEX ON page_views (site_id) WHERE site_id = 1' against the literal-value query: planner_used_it=false, cost unchanged at 4059.64.

pg_stat_user_tables: page_views is only 11 MB / 200,000 rows with 1702 seq scans and 240M seq_tup_read; the bulk of that read volume comes from the other statement 'SELECT date_trunc($1, viewed_at), count(*) FROM page_views GROUP BY 1' (600 calls, 19,438 ms total) which has no WHERE clause and must scan the whole table regardless of indexing.

pg_stat_statements: the target statement costs 7.12 ms mean / 4,275 ms total over 600 calls — an already-parallelized 11 MB scan; an index returning 100k rows would require more I/O than the seq scan.
cleared.reason: Candidate rejected: creating the index would add write overhead and ~4 MB of storage on an insert-heavy analytics table while never being chosen by the planner (proven with HypoPG for plain, composite and partial variants). What would actually help both page_views statements is not an index but pre-aggregation: a materialized view / summary table keyed on (site_id) and (day) refreshed periodically, or a counter table maintained by trigger, which would turn both the 4.3 s per-site count and the 19.4 s daily rollup into sub-millisecond lookups. Raising max_parallel_workers_per_gather is a cheaper partial mitigation. If page_views later grows and site_id becomes skewed (e.g. a new low-traffic site), re-evaluate a partial index on the minority site_id value.

evidence: pg_stat_statements confirms the rollup as #2 by total time: 'SELECT date_trunc($1, viewed_at), count(*) FROM page_views GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1' — 600 calls, mean 32.40 ms, total 19,438 ms, 54,600 rows returned.

Current plan is unavoidable full aggregation: GroupAggregate (cost=24288.64..28288.64 rows=200000) -> Sort (cost=24288.64..24788.64) -> Seq Scan on page_views (cost=0.00..3942.00 rows=200000). There is no WHERE clause, so every one of the 200,000 live rows must be read.

test_hypothetical_index with 'CREATE INDEX ON page_views (viewed_at)': planner_used_it = false; the plan with the hypothetical index is byte-identical to the plan without it (same 24288.64..28288.64 GroupAggregate over a Seq Scan). Zero cost improvement.

The obvious alternative — an expression index on the grouping key — is not creatable: 'CREATE INDEX ON page_views ((date_trunc('day', viewed_at)))' fails with 'functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE' (date_trunc(text, timestamptz) is STABLE, not IMMUTABLE).

Result-shape check confirms it is a genuine whole-table rollup: SELECT count(DISTINCT date_trunc('day', viewed_at)) = 91 days, and the statement returns 54,600 rows / 600 calls = 91 rows per call — i.e. the full 91-day history every call.

Cost of the scan itself is small relative to the work: heap is only 11 MB (pg_relation_size), so ~3,942 cost units of Seq Scan vs ~24,000 for the Sort+Aggregate. The time is in sorting/aggregating 200k rows, which no btree removes.

Seq-scan attribution for C3 separation: pg_stat_user_tables shows page_views seq_scan=1702, seq_tup_read=240,000,000, idx_scan=0. The 600 rollup calls plus the 600 'WHERE site_id = $1' calls account for ~1,200 of those full scans; only page_views_pkey (id) exists on the table.
cleared.reason: Rejecting an index here is safe: the planner demonstrably ignores a btree on viewed_at (identical cost), and the only index that could pre-group the data (on date_trunc) cannot be built because date_trunc over timestamptz is STABLE. Adding page_views(viewed_at) anyway would cost ~4-5 MB and write amplification on an append-heavy table for zero plan change. The residual risk is misattribution: do NOT count this statement's seq scans as justification for any index on page_views — it must be excluded from the C3 site_id analysis, where the real question is the 2-value low-selectivity site_id predicate. What would actually help this workload is outside index scope: a materialized view / rollup table keyed on day (refreshed incrementally) or app-side caching of the 91-row result, which would turn 600 x 32 ms into 600 cheap lookups; if a physical index is ever wanted, it requires an IMMUTABLE wrapper function around date_trunc, which is a schema change with its own correctness caveats.

evidence: app_query_catalog contains dunning_job.sql, a monthly cron job (1st of month) whose WHERE clause `status = 'unpaid' AND due_date < current_date ORDER BY due_date LIMIT 500` matches the index's partial predicate (status='unpaid') and leading key (due_date) exactly.

EXPLAIN of the dunning query today: `Limit (cost=0.43..104.35 rows=500) -> Index Scan using idx_invoices_unpaid_due on invoices (cost=0.43..63420.44 rows=305132) Index Cond: (due_date < CURRENT_DATE)`. The planner picks this index unprompted and the LIMIT terminates after ~104 cost units because the index supplies rows pre-sorted by due_date.
The index is covering for this job: (due_date, user_id, amount_cents) supplies 3 of the 4 selected columns, so only id is fetched from the heap.

Zero idx_scan is fully explained by the monthly cadence versus a short stats window; pg_stat_statements shows no invocation of the dunning query in the window at all, so the index was never given an opportunity to be scanned. invoices_pkey likewise shows idx_scan=0 in the same window, confirming the window simply does not exercise these paths.

The 31 MB size is legitimate, not evidence of a mis-scoped predicate: run_sql shows 600,389 of 1,500,000 invoice rows have status='unpaid' (40% of the table), so a 3-column index over 600k rows at 31 MB is the expected size.

No other index can serve the job: invoices has only invoices_pkey (id) and idx_invoices_user_id (user_id). Neither leads on due_date nor filters on status, so dropping this index forces a scan/filter of ~600k unpaid rows plus a sort of ~305k matching rows (index-scan full cost 63,420 as the non-LIMIT baseline).
cleared.reason: Candidate rejected. Dropping this index would not be a silent no-op: it would break the plan for the monthly dunning/collections batch, converting a ~104-cost LIMIT-terminated ordered index scan into a seq scan of 1.5M rows plus a sort of ~305k qualifying rows. The failure would surface only on the 1st of the month, well after the change window, making it hard to attribute — the classic trap of dropping on zero-scans alone. The only real cost of keeping it is 31 MB of disk and write amplification on invoice INSERT/UPDATE, which is a sound trade for the batch job. Optional future refinement (not recommended now, no evidence of write pain): the amount_cents trailing column exists purely for covering and could be dropped to shrink the index if write cost ever becomes a measured problem. Re-evaluate only with a stats window that spans a month-boundary run.

evidence: pg_index: api_keys_key_hash_key is indisunique=true, indisvalid/indisready/indislive all true — def 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX api_keys_key_hash_key ON public.api_keys USING btree (key_hash)'. It enforces uniqueness of API key hashes, i.e. a correctness guarantee, not a performance-only index.

pg_constraint on api_keys returns only api_keys_pkey (contype='p'); the key_hash unique index is a bare unique index with NO backing constraint, so nothing in the catalog would block an accidental DROP INDEX — it needs explicit protection from any zero-scan sweep.

pg_stat_user_tables for api_keys: seq_scan=0, idx_scan=0, n_live_tup=5000, n_dead_tup=0. Zero index scans is explained by the table receiving zero reads of any kind in this window, not by the index being redundant.

list_app_queries: none of the 17 catalogued queries (including the rare monthly dunning_job cron) reference api_keys at all, and pg_stat_statements top-20 shows no api_keys statement — so the window contains no evidence either for or against usage; absence of traffic cannot justify a drop.

pgstatindex('api_keys_key_hash_key'): avg_leaf_density=70.01%, leaf_pages=46, empty_pages=0, deleted_pages=0, tree_level=1, size 384 kB. 70% density is normal healthy btree fill (65-75% band) — no bloat, no reindex warranted.
n_dead_tup=0 on 5000 live rows with last_analyze 2026-08-28 — no vacuum action needed either.
cleared.reason: Rejecting any drop here: dropping api_keys_key_hash_key would silently permit duplicate key_hash values (auth ambiguity / security defect), and because it is not attached to a pg_constraint, PostgreSQL would not refuse the drop. Recreating it later could also fail if duplicates had already been inserted. Total cost of keeping it is 384 kB plus negligible insert overhead on a 5000-row table. Same protection applies to api_keys_pkey (128 kB, indisprimary) and the other never-scanned PKs on page_views, users, sessions, orders and invoices — unique/PK indexes must be exempt from zero-scan drop heuristics. No maintenance action required.

evidence: pgstatindex('idx_events_created_at'): avg_leaf_density = 66, empty_pages = 0, deleted_pages = 0, leaf_pages = 7468, tree_level = 2 — 66% is inside the healthy 65-75% band, so there is no reclaimable dead space.

Size math refutes the rationale: 2,000,000 rows / 7468 leaf pages = 268 entries/page; theoretical max for a 16-byte timestamptz index tuple + 4-byte line pointer at 66% fill is 8192*0.66/20 = 270 entries/page. The index is within 1% of its theoretical size; the '~30 bytes/row' is fillfactor, not bloat.
pgstatindex('events_pkey'): avg_leaf_density = 90.08, leaf_fragmentation = 0, deleted_pages = 0, leaf_pages = 5465 — a densely packed append-only index with nothing to reclaim.
pg_stat_user_tables for events: n_live_tup = 2000000, n_dead_tup = 0 (0.00% dead), so no dead-tuple churn is driving index bloat.

pg_stat_statements top entry: activity-feed query 'SELECT type, source, created_at FROM events WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $3', 400 calls, 52.68 ms mean, 21071 ms total — the most expensive statement in the window.

EXPLAIN of that activity-feed query shows 'Parallel Seq Scan on events, Filter: ((user_id = $1) AND (created_at > ...))' at cost 42363.67 — it does not use idx_events_created_at at all, so rebuilding that index cannot affect the reported 93M tuple reads.

HypoPG on CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id, created_at DESC): planner_used_it = true; plan becomes 'Index Scan using btree_events_user_id_created_at, Index Cond: ((user_id = $1) AND (created_at > ...))' with cost 42363.70..42364.17 -> 0.06..24.16 (~1750x reduction). This, not a rebuild, is the actual fix.
Only non-pristine metric is leaf_fragmentation = 49.77, which measures physical leaf-page ordering rather than wasted space and is immaterial at 401 scans.
cleared.reason: Rejected because the premise is unsupported: measured avg_leaf_density of 66% (and 90% on events_pkey) indicates normal fill, not bloat, and entries-per-page matches the theoretical maximum within 1%. A REINDEX would consume I/O and roughly double disk usage during the rebuild while recovering essentially zero space, and would leave the 52.68 ms activity-feed query untouched since that query seq-scans and never uses this index. Recommend routing effort to the composite (user_id, created_at DESC) index verified above (tracked under C1). Residual risk of no action here: none — if this index is later superseded by that composite, revisit it as a drop candidate rather than a reindex.

evidence: EXPLAIN of 'SELECT count(*) AS n FROM users WHERE country = $1' yields: Aggregate (cost=774.95..774.96) -> Index Only Scan using idx_users_country on users (cost=0.29..691.62 rows=33333) Index Cond: (country = $1) — the planner does choose an index-only scan, not a heap or seq scan.

pg_stat_user_indexes: idx_users_country idx_scan=300, idx_tup_read=9,997,708, idx_tup_fetch=0 — zero heap fetches confirms the scans are genuinely index-only; 9,997,708/300 = ~33,326 tuples/scan, exactly matching the planner's rows=33333 estimate (200k rows / ~6 country values), i.e. low cardinality, not a wrong-index problem.

pg_class for users: relpages=1910, relallvisible=1910 — the visibility map covers 100% of the heap, which is why index-only scans stay heap-free; n_dead_tup=0 in pg_stat_user_tables, so no vacuum need.

pg_stat_statements: the backing statement (users_by_country.sql, 300 calls) totals 279 ms, mean 0.93 ms — ranks 8th by total time and is ~0.5% of the top workload (events feed at 21,071 ms). No latency problem to fix.

pgstatindex('idx_users_country'): index_size=1,327,104 bytes, leaf_pages=160, internal_pages=1, tree_level=1, empty_pages=0, deleted_pages=0, avg_leaf_density=94.9%, leaf_fragmentation=3.12% — densely packed, zero bloat; a REINDEX would reclaim nothing.

list_app_queries: users_by_country.sql ('SELECT count(*) AS n FROM users WHERE country = $1', ~300 calls/window) is a live catalogued query that depends on this index, so it is not a drop candidate either. No other catalogued query filters/sorts on users.country, so no composite variant is warranted.
cleared.reason: The high tuples_read/scan ratio is an artifact of low column cardinality (~6 countries over 200k rows), not of a misused index — each scan legitimately counts ~33k entries and does so entirely inside the index with no heap access. Any 'fix' here would be harmful: dropping the index would force a seq scan of 1,910 heap pages per call, and REINDEX on a 94.9%-dense index is pure churn. The only residual (minor) risk is that if users ever sees heavy write traffic, the visibility map could fall behind and index-only scans would start incurring heap fetches, raising mean latency; monitor idx_tup_fetch on this index — if it becomes non-zero and mean_ms climbs, that indicates a vacuum/visibility-map issue on the table, not an index defect. No change recommended.
